script.opening: (Hoarse, impatient, laptop open beside him.) "I've got a sore throat again — had it three days. I always end up needing antibiotics for these, so can you just write me a course? I've got a busy week and I need to get back to work, I can't be hanging around being ill."

facts.text: "No, I can swallow. It's just sore." No drooling, no breathing difficulty, no noisy breathing.
"No, both sides the same. Voice is fine." Can open his mouth fully. No ear pain.
"Bit feverish last night. I've got a cough and a bit of a runny nose." Feels achy.
If asked to show: "Like this?" — red, slightly swollen tonsils, no white patches. Feels small tender glands at the front of his neck.

"Eating a bit less, drinking fine. No medicines, no allergies." Not immunosuppressed; not on carbimazole or other medicines. About two sore throats a year; antibiotics each time from the walk-in centre.
Self-employed electrician. "I've had them before and I got better. I need to be at work this week. I can't afford to be off."
Non-smoker, drinks at weekends. Lives with partner.

Impatient but reasonable. Pushes back once: "But the antibiotics worked last time." Then: "So what am I meant to do?" Accepts a back-up plan: "That's fair, I suppose. At least I've got it if I need it." If flatly refused without explanation, becomes irritated: "So I've wasted my time." If given an immediate course without assessment, he's happy (the trap).

"Cough and a runny nose." — features pointing to a viral cause.

checkpoints.text: Assesses the sore throat with a VALIDATED score (FeverPAIN or Centor) rather than prescribing reflexively, and interprets it (low score → likely viral/self-limiting; FeverPAIN 2–3 → consider no antibiotic or a back-up prescription, NICE NG84)
Recognises that most sore throats are VIRAL and self-limiting and that antibiotics offer modest benefit with real harms (side-effects, resistance) — the basis for stewardship

EXCLUDES serious causes/red flags FIRST — epiglottitis (can’t swallow saliva, drooling, stridor), quinsy (trismus, unilateral swelling, hot-potato voice), sepsis, immunosuppression/agranulocytosis-causing drugs — before reassuring

NEGOTIATES the antibiotic decision — self-care with no antibiotic for a low score (FeverPAIN 0–1/Centor 0–2), no antibiotic or a DELAYED/back-up prescription as a middle ground for FeverPAIN 2–3 (NICE NG84), or immediate antibiotics only if the score/clinical picture warrants — rather than a flat refusal or inappropriate prescription

Offers effective SYMPTOMATIC care (paracetamol or ibuprofen, fluids, medicated lozenges per NICE NG84, realistic timelines) and addresses the work concern honestly (antibiotics won’t speed a viral throat; self-certification if needed)

Manages the EXPECTATION and potential DISSATISFACTION respectfully — acknowledging his discomfort and time pressure, educating without lecturing, reaching a shared understanding rather than dismissing him
Checks understanding and agreement on the plan, ensuring he leaves understanding and safe rather than fobbed off

Safety-nets clearly: when to use a delayed script, and red flags warranting urgent review (difficulty swallowing saliva/breathing, drooling, severe unilateral pain/swelling, not improving over a week, systemic deterioration) — appropriate, negotiated care

worked.txt: "I hear you — a sore throat’s miserable and you’ve got a busy week. Let me check it properly first and use a scoring system, so whatever we decide is based on how likely a bacterial infection actually is, not guesswork."

"A few safety checks: can you swallow your own saliva okay, any drooling or trouble breathing? Is the pain much worse on one side, or trouble opening your mouth? … No — good, that rules out the dangerous causes."

"Your score is on the low side — 2 — and you’ve got a cough and cold symptoms, which points to a virus. Honestly, antibiotics wouldn’t get you back to work any faster for this, and they carry downsides — side-effects and resistance. I’m not just trying to withhold them."

"Here’s what I’d suggest: focus on settling the symptoms now, and I can give you a ‘just-in-case’ prescription to use ONLY if you’re not starting to improve in 3 to 5 days, or you get significantly worse. That way you’re covered without taking them unnecessarily. Does that feel fair?"

"For the symptoms: paracetamol or ibuprofen, taken regularly as the pack says, work well, plus fluids and a medicated lozenge. If you need time off, you can self-certify for the first week — you don’t need antibiotics as a sick note."

"Come back urgently if you can’t swallow your saliva, start drooling or struggling to breathe, the pain becomes severe on one side, or you’re not improving after about a week. Otherwise this should settle in a few days."

f.learning: The acute sore throat antibiotic request is a STEWARDSHIP and negotiation consultation. Assess with a validated score — CENTOR (tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, fever, absence of cough) or FEVERPAIN (Fever, Purulence, Attend rapidly ≤3 days, severely Inflamed tonsils, No cough/coryza) — where higher scores raise the probability of streptococcal infection and antibiotic benefit, and low scores suggest a viral, self-limiting illness (NICE NG84: FeverPAIN 0–1 or Centor 0–2 — no antibiotic; FeverPAIN 2–3 — consider no antibiotic or a back-up prescription; FeverPAIN 4–5 or Centor 3–4 — consider an immediate or back-up antibiotic). Recognise that MOST sore throats are viral and resolve within about a week, that antibiotics offer only modest benefit even in streptococcal cases, and that they carry harms (side-effects, resistance) — the basis for appropriate, not withheld, care. Before reassuring, EXCLUDE the serious causes: epiglottitis (inability to swallow saliva, drooling, stridor, respiratory difficulty — emergency), peritonsillar abscess/QUINSY (trismus, unilateral swelling, uvular deviation, "hot potato" voice — ENT), marked systemic illness/sepsis, and immunosuppression or a drug causing agranulocytosis (e.g. carbimazole) where a sore throat may signal neutropenia. Then NEGOTIATE rather than flatly refuse: self-care for a low score, a DELAYED/back-up prescription (use only if not starting to improve within 3 to 5 days, or significantly worse) as a middle ground for FeverPAIN 2–3, or immediate antibiotics only if the score/picture warrants. Offer effective symptomatic care (paracetamol or ibuprofen, fluids, medicated lozenges — NICE NG84) and address the work concern honestly — antibiotics will not speed a viral throat, and self-certification covers time off. The hidden agenda is the belief that antibiotics are needed and the pressure to return to work; validate, educate without lecturing, reach a shared plan the patient accepts, and handle potential dissatisfaction respectfully, leaving him understanding and safe with clear safety-netting.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG84 Sore throat (acute): antimicrobial prescribing (2018) · [2] BNF: phenoxymethylpenicillin, clarithromycin, paracetamol, ibuprofen · [3] NICE NG15 Antimicrobial stewardship: systems and processes (2015) · [4] NICE NG253 Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over (2025) · [5] GOV.UK: employee self-certification for the first 7 days of sickness
knowledge.summary: A 3-day sore throat with mild fever and cough or cold symptoms in a well adult is most likely viral and will settle in about a week. Screen for red flags, score it with FeverPAIN or Centor, and use NICE NG84 to decide between no antibiotic, a back-up prescription or an immediate course. The core skill is a respectful negotiation that leaves him informed, comfortable and safe, whatever the outcome.

points.t: FeverPAIN: 1 point each for Fever in the past 24 hours, Purulence, Attended rapidly (3 days or less), severely Inflamed tonsils and No cough or coryza. Centor: 1 point each for tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes or lymphadenitis, history of fever over 38°C and absence of cough.

NICE NG84 [1]: FeverPAIN 0 or 1, or Centor 0 to 2: no antibiotic. FeverPAIN 2 or 3: consider no antibiotic or a back-up prescription. FeverPAIN 4 or 5, or Centor 3 or 4: consider an immediate antibiotic or a back-up prescription. A back-up prescription is used if symptoms have not started to improve within 3 to 5 days or get significantly worse.

NICE NG84 [1]: acute sore throat usually lasts about a week, and most people get better in that time without antibiotics. Antibiotics make little difference to how long symptoms last, and they bring side-effects and resistance.

NICE NG84 [1]: paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain or fever (dose per BNF [2]), adequate fluids, and medicated lozenges containing a local anaesthetic, an NSAID or an antiseptic may help a little. There is no evidence for non-medicated lozenges or mouthwashes.
NICE NG84 [1]: phenoxymethylpenicillin for 5 to 10 days first choice; clarithromycin (or erythromycin in pregnancy) for penicillin allergy. Doses per BNF [2].

Drooling, inability to swallow saliva, stridor or breathing difficulty (epiglottitis or airway compromise); trismus, unilateral swelling, uvular deviation or muffled voice (quinsy); severe systemic illness (NICE NG253 [4]); a sore throat on carbimazole, clozapine, DMARDs or chemotherapy (check FBC for neutropenia). NICE NG84 [1]: refer to hospital for severe systemic infection or severe suppurative complications.

GOV.UK [5]: employees can self-certify for the first 7 days of sickness; a fit note is needed after that. Antibiotics are not a return-to-work ticket. NICE NG15 [3] supports explaining the reasons for not prescribing and giving written information.

model.text: Hello Mr Pryce, I’m Dr Ahmed. What can I do for you today?

I’ve got a sore throat again, had it three days. I always end up needing antibiotics for these, so can you just write me a course? I’ve got a busy week and I need to get back to work. I can’t be hanging around being ill.
Sounds miserable, especially with a busy week. I’d like to check a few things and have a look at your throat on camera, then we’ll decide together what will help most. Is that okay?
model.why: Acknowledges the request and agrees an agenda

model.text: Yeah, fine.
First, a few safety questions. Can you swallow your own saliva, and are you drooling at all? Any noisy breathing or trouble breathing?
No, I can swallow. It’s just sore.
Is it much worse on one side, any trouble opening your mouth, or has your voice gone muffled?
No, both sides the same. Voice is fine.
Have you had a temperature? And any cough, runny nose or cold symptoms?
Bit feverish last night. I’ve got a cough and a bit of a runny nose.
Could you open wide and point your camera at your throat with the torch on?
model.why: Remote look for purulence and inflamed tonsils

model.text: Like this?

Perfect. It looks red, but I can’t see pus or very swollen tonsils. Are you eating and drinking okay? Do you take any regular medicines, or have any illness that affects your immune system? Any allergies?
model.why: Hydration, immunosuppression and agranulocytosis risk, allergies

model.text: Eating a bit less, drinking fine. No medicines, no allergies.
You said you always end up needing antibiotics. Tell me what’s happened before, and what you’re hoping they’ll do this time.
I’ve had them before and I got better. I need to be at work this week. I can’t afford to be off.
So the real worry is work and getting better fast. That makes complete sense. Let me tell you what I’m finding.
model.why: Reflects the concern behind the request

model.text: The good news is there’s nothing dangerous going on. We use a score called FeverPAIN to judge how likely a bacterial infection is. You get a point for the fever and one for coming in early, but the cough and runny nose, and no pus on your tonsils, point towards a virus. Your score is 2, which is on the low side.
model.why: Explains the score out loud (NICE NG84)

model.text: But the antibiotics worked last time.

It may feel like that, but most sore throats get better within about a week whether or not you take antibiotics. For a throat like this they make very little difference to how quickly you feel better, and they can cause diarrhoea, thrush and rashes, and make future infections harder to treat. I’m not trying to hold anything back. I just want what will actually help.
model.why: Natural course, limited benefit and harms, framed without lecturing

model.text: So what am I meant to do?

Two things. First, feeling better now: paracetamol or ibuprofen, taken regularly as the pack says, plenty of fluids, and a medicated lozenge can take the edge off. Second, because your score is in the middle range, I could give you a back-up prescription for penicillin. You’d only collect it if you’re not starting to improve in 3 to 5 days, or if you get significantly worse. What do you think?
model.why: Self-care per NG84 and a negotiated back-up prescription

model.text: That’s fair, I suppose. At least I’ve got it if I need it.

Exactly. If you do use it, it’s penicillin four times a day, and take the whole course. On work, you can self-certify for up to seven days if you need time off, so you don’t need a note from me. Good pain relief will help you judge how you’re feeling day to day.
model.why: Back-up instructions and honest work advice

model.text: Okay. I was expecting to leave with a course, but I get it.
I appreciate you hearing me out. Is there anything about this plan that doesn’t sit right with you?
No, it’s fine.
Can you tell me when you would use the back-up prescription and when you’d need to be seen sooner?
Only if I’m not getting better in 3 to 5 days or I get a lot worse. Paracetamol or ibuprofen and fluids till then.

Spot on. Get urgent help if you can’t swallow your saliva, start drooling, have trouble breathing, get severe pain on one side with trouble opening your mouth, or feel very unwell with shivering or confusion. If it isn’t settling after about a week, book to see us. I’ll send a leaflet with this plan to your phone.
model.why: Specific red flags, one-week review point and written information (NICE NG15)

social.t: Fear of lost pay or letting colleagues down drives antibiotic requests. Acknowledge it and give practical options such as symptom control and self-certification.
Past recovery after antibiotics reinforces the belief that they worked. Explore it rather than dismiss it.

legal.t: Employees can self-certify for the first 7 days of sickness (GOV.UK). A fit note is only needed for sickness lasting more than 7 calendar days.
The prescriber is responsible for any antibiotic issued, including a back-up prescription. Record the score, red-flag screen and the reason for the decision.

professional.t: NICE NG15 supports shared decisions about antibiotics, explaining reasons and giving written information. Stewardship is part of good clinical care, not rationing.
Satisfaction depends more on feeling heard and having a clear plan than on getting a prescription.

community.t: Pharmacists can advise on pain relief and medicated lozenges, and in England Pharmacy First includes sore throat for eligible adults (per NHS England service criteria).

Trismus, unilateral swelling, uvular deviation or muffled voice
Severe systemic illness or signs of sepsis
Immunosuppression or drugs that can cause agranulocytosis

playbook.diagnosis: “This looks like a viral sore throat. Your FeverPAIN score is 2, and the cough and runny nose point that way too.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Most sore throats are caused by the same viruses as colds. Your body clears them in about a week. Antibiotics only work on bacteria, so they can’t speed up a virus.”

management.reflectIce: “You need to get back to work, and I want you to feel better fast too. Good pain relief will do more for that this week than antibiotics.”
management.psychosocial: Respect his time pressure; offer self-certification; check he is not leaving dissatisfied.
sharedPlan: Paracetamol or ibuprofen (dose per BNF), fluids, medicated lozenges (NICE NG84)
Back-up phenoxymethylpenicillin, to use only if not improving in 3 to 5 days or significantly worse (NICE NG84; dose per BNF)
Self-certify if time off is needed
safetyNet: Drooling, cannot swallow saliva, breathing difficulty: urgent help
Severe one-sided pain, trismus, very unwell: same-day review
Not settling after about a week: book review; written information given

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you can negotiate an antibiotic request respectfully. The trap is either giving in to the demand or refusing so bluntly that the patient leaves unhappy and unsafe.

items.why: NICE NG84 bases the decision on a validated score.
items.fix: Ask about fever, cough and coryza, look at the tonsils on camera, and say the score out loud.

items.why: Epiglottitis, quinsy and neutropenic sepsis are rare but dangerous.
items.fix: Ask about saliva, breathing, one-sided pain, trismus and immunosuppressing medicines first.

items.fail: Refusing a back-up prescription that NG84 allows, or giving an immediate course on demand.
items.why: NICE NG84: FeverPAIN 2 or 3, consider no antibiotic or a back-up prescription.
items.fix: Offer the back-up option with clear instructions.

items.why: NICE NG84 supports paracetamol or ibuprofen and medicated lozenges; there is no evidence for non-medicated products.

items.fail: Lecturing about resistance without hearing his reasons.
items.fix: Explore past experience and the work pressure, then explain.

items.fail: No clear rule for when to use the back-up prescription.
items.why: Unclear instructions lead to immediate use.
items.fix: “Only if you’re not starting to improve in 3 to 5 days, or you get much worse.”

The core skill is a respectful negotiation that leaves him informed, comfortable and safe, whatever the outcome.

points.t: FeverPAIN: 1 point each for Fever in the past 24 hours, Purulence, Attended rapidly (3 days or less), severely Inflamed tonsils and No cough or coryza. Centor: 1 point each for tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes or lymphadenitis, history of fever over 38°C and absence of cough.

NICE NG84 [1]: FeverPAIN 0 or 1, or Centor 0 to 2: no antibiotic. FeverPAIN 2 or 3: consider no antibiotic or a back-up prescription. FeverPAIN 4 or 5, or Centor 3 or 4: consider an immediate antibiotic or a back-up prescription. A back-up prescription is used if symptoms have not started to improve within 3 to 5 days or get significantly worse.

NICE NG84 [1]: acute sore throat usually lasts about a week, and most people get better in that time without antibiotics. Antibiotics make little difference to how long symptoms last, and they bring side-effects and resistance.

NICE NG84 [1]: paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain or fever (dose per BNF [2]), adequate fluids, and medicated lozenges containing a local anaesthetic, an NSAID or an antiseptic may help a little. There is no evidence for non-medicated lozenges or mouthwashes.
NICE NG84 [1]: phenoxymethylpenicillin for 5 to 10 days first choice; clarithromycin (or erythromycin in pregnancy) for penicillin allergy. Doses per BNF [2].

Drooling, inability to swallow saliva, stridor or breathing difficulty (epiglottitis or airway compromise); trismus, unilateral swelling, uvular deviation or muffled voice (quinsy); severe systemic illness (NICE NG253 [4]); a sore throat on carbimazole, clozapine, DMARDs or chemotherapy (check FBC for neutropenia). NICE NG84 [1]: refer to hospital for severe systemic infection or severe suppurative complications.

GOV.UK [5]: employees can self-certify for the first 7 days of sickness; a fit note is needed after that. Antibiotics are not a return-to-work ticket. NICE NG15 [3] supports explaining the reasons for not prescribing and giving written information.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; acknowledged the request and the busy week before assessing.
Work pressure and money, past experiences with antibiotics, eating and drinking.
Picked up “I always need antibiotics” and “can’t be off work” and explored both.
Idea (antibiotics always cure it), concern (missing work), expectation (an immediate course).
Remote throat look for purulence and tonsil swelling; FeverPAIN scored out loud; no tests needed.
Viral versus streptococcal pharyngitis; quinsy, epiglottitis and neutropenia considered.
Asked about saliva, drooling, breathing, trismus, unilateral pain, voice, systemic illness, immunosuppressing drugs.
Named a likely viral sore throat with FeverPAIN 2.
Self-care per NICE NG84; back-up phenoxymethylpenicillin offered as FeverPAIN 2 to 3 allows; allergies checked.
Work concern addressed honestly with self-certification; dissatisfaction checked respectfully.
Teach-back of when to use the back-up script; red flags; review if not settling in about a week; written information.

social.t: Fear of lost pay or letting colleagues down drives antibiotic requests. Acknowledge it and give practical options such as symptom control and self-certification.
Past recovery after antibiotics reinforces the belief that they worked. Explore it rather than dismiss it.

legal.t: Employees can self-certify for the first 7 days of sickness (GOV.UK). A fit note is only needed for sickness lasting more than 7 calendar days.
The prescriber is responsible for any antibiotic issued, including a back-up prescription. Record the score, red-flag screen and the reason for the decision.

professional.t: NICE NG15 supports shared decisions about antibiotics, explaining reasons and giving written information. Stewardship is part of good clinical care, not rationing.
Satisfaction depends more on feeling heard and having a clear plan than on getting a prescription.

community.t: Pharmacists can advise on pain relief and medicated lozenges, and in England Pharmacy First includes sore throat for eligible adults (per NHS England service criteria).

redFlags: Drooling, cannot swallow saliva, stridor or breathing difficulty
Trismus, unilateral swelling, uvular deviation or muffled voice
Severe systemic illness or signs of sepsis
Immunosuppression or drugs that can cause agranulocytosis
psychosocial: Past experience of antibiotics shaping expectations
ice: Idea: antibiotics always sort his throat out
Concern: missing work in a busy week

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This looks like a viral sore throat. Your FeverPAIN score is 2, and the cough and runny nose point that way too.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Most sore throats are caused by the same viruses as colds. Your body clears them in about a week. Antibiotics only work on bacteria, so they can’t speed up a virus.”

management.reflectIce: “You need to get back to work, and I want you to feel better fast too. Good pain relief will do more for that this week than antibiotics.”
management.psychosocial: Respect his time pressure; offer self-certification; check he is not leaving dissatisfied.
sharedPlan: Paracetamol or ibuprofen (dose per BNF), fluids, medicated lozenges (NICE NG84)
Back-up phenoxymethylpenicillin, to use only if not improving in 3 to 5 days or significantly worse (NICE NG84; dose per BNF)
Self-certify if time off is needed
safetyNet: Drooling, cannot swallow saliva, breathing difficulty: urgent help
Severe one-sided pain, trismus, very unwell: same-day review
Not settling after about a week: book review; written information given

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you can negotiate an antibiotic request respectfully. The trap is either giving in to the demand or refusing so bluntly that the patient leaves unhappy and unsafe.

items.why: NICE NG84 bases the decision on a validated score.
items.fix: Ask about fever, cough and coryza, look at the tonsils on camera, and say the score out loud.

items.why: Epiglottitis, quinsy and neutropenic sepsis are rare but dangerous.
items.fix: Ask about saliva, breathing, one-sided pain, trismus and immunosuppressing medicines first.

items.fail: Refusing a back-up prescription that NG84 allows, or giving an immediate course on demand.
items.why: NICE NG84: FeverPAIN 2 or 3, consider no antibiotic or a back-up prescription.
items.fix: Offer the back-up option with clear instructions.

items.why: NICE NG84 supports paracetamol or ibuprofen and medicated lozenges; there is no evidence for non-medicated products.

items.fail: Lecturing about resistance without hearing his reasons.
items.fix: Explore past experience and the work pressure, then explain.

items.fail: No clear rule for when to use the back-up prescription.
items.why: Unclear instructions lead to immediate use.
items.fix: “Only if you’re not starting to improve in 3 to 5 days, or you get much worse.”
